title: What Happens to a Sandwich
principle: Taking food apart into pieces small enough to cross is called digestion.

t: You eat bread and cheese. A day later some of it is you. None of it arrived as bread or cheese.
Nothing you eat is absorbed as what it was. A sandwich is dismantled to its component monomers before any of it crosses into you, and what gets built afterwards is yours.
sub: You have met the reason twice already — once as size, once as specification.

t: Taking food apart into pieces small enough to cross is called digestion.
Digestion is hydrolysis: polymers cut back into the monomers they were built from — starch to glucose, protein to amino acids, fat to fatty acids.
It is the exact reverse of the polymerisation you met in Biomolecules, run by enzymes, and it reduces everything to a common currency of monomers.

That reduction to a common currency is why any organism can eat any other. Nothing about a cow's protein is retained; it becomes amino acids indistinguishable from those in a lentil, and you rebuild from the pool. Digestion is not purification and not extraction — it is standardisation.
sub: Nothing you eat becomes part of you as it was.
You do not absorb a cow's proteins. You absorb amino acids and build your own.
Which is why an intact protein slipping across the barrier is exactly what the immune system treats as an intruder.

That is food allergy: the system is not malfunctioning, it is responding correctly to a protein that should never have arrived intact. It also explains why allergies cluster on the foods whose proteins most resist digestion — peanut, shellfish, egg.

q: Why can insulin not be swallowed?
Why must protein drugs be injected?
Why is oral delivery of peptide drugs such a persistent problem?
options: It is a protein, and the gut takes proteins apart
It would be absorbed too fast
why: Your gut cannot tell the difference between insulin and any other protein. It takes it apart into amino acids, and amino acids do not do what insulin does.

The gut is built to dismantle proteins indiscriminately, and it has no way to recognise a therapeutic one. This is the delivery problem, not a chemistry problem — the drug has been available since 1982 and still requires a needle.

Because the barrier that keeps foreign proteins out is the same barrier a protein drug must cross, and it cannot be selectively relaxed. Enormous effort has gone into enteric coatings, absorption enhancers and enzyme inhibitors, and oral insulin remains largely unsolved — the two requirements are in direct opposition.

t: It is why your small intestine is folded until it has the surface area of a tennis court.

Absorption depends on area, so the tube is folded, the folds carry villi, and the villi carry microvilli — three levels turning a few metres into around 30 square metres. Coeliac disease damages that surface, and the consequence is malnutrition despite an adequate diet: the problem is not the food and not the tube, it is the area.
